label: Landmark Supreme Court Judgments
blurb: A comprehensive compilation of landmark Supreme Court judgments that have shaped Indian constitutional law. These cases are essential for understanding the evolution of fundamental rights, basic structure, federalism, and judicial review.

topics.title: SR Bommai v Union of India and Article 356
topics.hook: The Supreme Court restricted the arbitrary use of Article 356 by the central government, establishing federalism and secularism as basic features.
topics.story:
The SR Bommai judgement (1994) is the defining ruling on Article 356 of the Constitution of India, which allows the imposition of President's Rule in states. The case arose after the dismissal of the Janata Dal government in Karnataka led by S.R. Bommai in 1989. The Governor dismissed the government without giving Bommai a chance to prove his majority on the floor of the assembly. Several other state governments were also dismissed around this time, leading to a consolidated batch of petitions before a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court.

The Court held that the power of the President to dismiss a state government is not absolute. It is subject to judicial review. If the Court finds that the dismissal was based on irrelevant or mala fide grounds, it can strike down the Presidential proclamation. The Court's detailed guidelines mandated that the President can only suspend the assembly upon issuing the proclamation, and dissolution can only occur after parliamentary approval. This procedural safeguard prevented the Centre from presenting a fait accompli to Parliament. Importantly, the Court ruled that the floor of the assembly is the only place to test a majority, stopping the practice of Governors deciding a Chief Minister's strength based on subjective reports.

The judgement also classified federalism and secularism as part of the basic structure of the Constitution. A state government acting against secularism can be dismissed, as happened to four BJP state governments after the demolition of the Babri Masjid in 1992. The Court upheld those dismissals while invalidating others.

Before Bommai, Article 356 was frequently misused to topple opposition governments. Since 1994, the frequency of President's Rule has dropped significantly. The ruling shifted power back to elected state assemblies and made the floor test an unskippable requirement for proving confidence.

facts.v: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India

topics.why: CLAT usually tests the relationship between the Centre and states. The examiner will likely focus on the basic structure additions (secularism) or the floor test principle.

topics.title: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v Shah Bano Begum and Muslim Personal Law
topics.hook: The Supreme Court upheld a divorced Muslim woman's right to maintenance under Section 125 of the CrPC, sparking a political backlash and legislative override.
topics.story:
In 1932, Shah Bano married Mohd. Ahmed Khan. Decades later, Khan divorced her and refused to pay regular maintenance. Shah Bano filed a petition under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which compels men to maintain their wives, children, and parents if they are unable to maintain themselves. Khan argued that under Muslim personal law, his obligation ended with the iddat period (roughly three months).

A five-judge Supreme Court bench ruled in 1985 that Section 125 is a secular provision. It applies to all citizens regardless of their religion. The Court held that if there is a conflict between personal law and Section 125, the secular criminal law prevails. The judgement affirmed Shah Bano's right to maintenance beyond the iddat period, citing the Quran to state that providing for a divorced wife is a religious duty as well. The judges argued that true religion cannot conflict with social justice.

The ruling caused a massive uproar among orthodox Muslim groups who saw it as interference in personal laws. The Rajiv Gandhi government, holding a massive majority in Parliament, bowed to the conservative backlash. They passed the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986. This law essentially nullified the Supreme Court judgement by restricting a divorced Muslim woman's right to maintenance from her former husband to the iddat period alone. The burden of maintenance was shifted to her relatives or the Wakf Board.

The political capitulation remains a debated episode in Indian history, often cited as a failure to enact a Uniform Civil Code under Article 44. Subsequent judgements, like Danial Latifi (2001), have reinterpreted the 1986 Act to require a husband to make a fair provision for the entire future within the iddat period, practically reviving the Shah Bano principle.

facts.v: Section 125 is secular and applies to all religions
Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986
Danial Latifi v. Union of India (2001)

topics.why: The conflict between secular criminal law and personal law is a regular CLAT theme. Questions often target the 1986 Act and the political aftermath.

topics.title: Shayara Bano v Union of India and the End of Triple Talaq
topics.hook: A five-judge bench struck down the practice of instant triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat) as unconstitutional and arbitrary.
topics.story:
Shayara Bano was married for 15 years before her husband divorced her by pronouncing 'talaq' three times in a letter. She challenged the practice of talaq-e-biddat (instant triple talaq), polygamy, and nikah halala in the Supreme Court. The Court decided to focus solely on talaq-e-biddat, leaving the issues of polygamy and nikah halala for future consideration. They formed a five-judge multi-faith bench to hear the matter.

In a 3:2 majority ruling in 2017, the Court declared instant triple talaq unconstitutional. The reasoning varied among the majority judges. Justices Rohinton Nariman and U.U. Lalit held that the practice is manifestly arbitrary and violates Article 14 (right to equality). They noted that the practice allows a man to break marital ties whimsically and capriciously, without any attempt at reconciliation. Justice Kurian Joseph concurred in the outcome but reasoned that instant triple talaq lacks legal sanction in Islamic theology itself, meaning it is not protected by personal law.

Chief Justice J.S. Khehar and Justice S. Abdul Nazeer dissented. They argued that personal laws are protected under Article 25 (freedom of religion) and cannot be tested against fundamental rights. They directed the Parliament to frame a law instead.

Following the judgement, the Union government passed the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019. This law criminalised the pronouncement of instant triple talaq, making it a cognizable and non-bailable offence carrying a jail term of up to three years. The criminalisation of a civil wrong remains a matter of legal debate, with critics arguing that jailing the husband defeats the purpose of securing maintenance for the wife.

topics.why: Passages usually focus on the concept of 'manifest arbitrariness' introduced by Justice Nariman or the debate around criminalising a civil wrong.

topics.title: Vishaka v State of Rajasthan and Workplace Harassment Guidelines
topics.hook: In the absence of legislation, the Supreme Court laid down binding guidelines to prevent and redress sexual harassment of women at the workplace.
topics.story:
The Vishaka case arose from the brutal gang-rape of Bhanwari Devi, a social worker in Rajasthan who was trying to stop child marriages as part of a government programme. The trial court acquitted the accused, prompting outrage. Several women's rights groups filed public interest litigations in the Supreme Court, highlighting the complete absence of laws to protect working women from harassment.

In 1997, the Supreme Court acknowledged that sexual harassment at the workplace violates the fundamental rights to equality (Article 14), life and liberty (Article 21), and the right to practice any profession (Article 19(1)(g)). Recognising the legislative vacuum, the Court used its powers under Article 141 and Article 32 to lay down the 'Vishaka Guidelines'. The Court explicitly drew upon international conventions, particularly the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), to interpret the fundamental rights, noting that international treaties can be read into domestic law if they do not conflict with it.

The guidelines defined sexual harassment broadly, covering physical contact, demands for sexual favours, sexually coloured remarks, and any other unwelcome physical, verbal, or non-verbal conduct of a sexual nature. They made it mandatory for employers to provide a safe working environment and required the establishment of an Internal Complaints Committee (ICC) in workplaces, headed by a woman and including an external member, to hear grievances.

These judicially created guidelines functioned as law for 16 years. In 2013, the Parliament finally enacted the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act (POSH Act), which codified and expanded upon the Vishaka Guidelines.
topics.why: The use of international treaties to interpret domestic fundamental rights is a regular exam topic. The structure of the ICC under the POSH Act is also frequently tested.

topics.title: KS Puttaswamy v Union of India and the Right to Privacy
topics.hook: A unanimous nine-judge bench ruled that the right to privacy is an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21.
topics.story:
The challenge to the Aadhaar project led to one of the most significant constitutional rulings in Indian history. When petitioners argued that mandatory biometric collection for Aadhaar violated the right to privacy, the Union government claimed that the Constitution does not guarantee any fundamental right to privacy, relying on older judgements like MP Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962). To resolve this, a nine-judge bench was formed.

In August 2017, the Supreme Court unanimously declared that privacy is a fundamental right. It is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21, and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution. The judgement expressly overruled the earlier decisions in MP Sharma and Kharak Singh. It encompasses spatial privacy, decisional autonomy, and informational privacy.

The Court clarified that the right to privacy is not absolute. Any restriction on privacy by the State must pass a three-pronged test: it must be backed by a valid law, pursue a legitimate state aim, and be proportionate to the objective sought. This proportionality test has since become the standard for assessing state intrusions into personal liberties.

The Puttaswamy judgement shifted Indian jurisprudence. By establishing privacy as a fundamental right, it laid the groundwork for subsequent rulings, including the decriminalisation of homosexuality in Navtej Singh Johar (2018) and the striking down of the adultery law in Joseph Shine (2018). It also forced the government to draft comprehensive data protection legislation, eventually resulting in the Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023.

facts.v: Aadhaar challenge leading to privacy ruling

topics.why: It is the bedrock of modern fundamental rights jurisprudence in India. The proportionality test and the cases it overruled are prime material for MCQs.
